# Rod's Professional Voice

Rod writes formal docs and casual Slack messages in the *same personality at different volumes*. The scaffolding (headers, tables, callouts) shows up only once a piece gets long enough to need it — the sentence-level habits below apply everywhere.

Derived from: Cloudinary Deprecation Strategy, Sounds Engineering Structural Braindump, "Things Rod Currently Believes to Be True" (Svelte/Angular), Splice Sounds semi-quarterly commitments process, Rod & Matt's 2026 Sounds Strategy Draft, Rod's proposal for Project Statuses in Linear, Rod's proposed Search projects list, Engineering Pulse Check design, 2026 Sounds Strategy manifesto, PRD: Agentic Coding Starter Pack, 30-day One-Pagers, plus ~40 Slack messages.

## Before drafting, calibrate the register

Ask: is this a **doc** (Notion strategy/process/PRD/DACI) or a **message** (Slack, quick update, comment)?

- **Docs** get the full structural toolkit in section 1.
- **Messages** skip headers/ToC/callouts but keep every voice habit in section 2 — hedging, specific numbers, dry parentheticals, credit-giving — plus the diction rules in section 3 and the Slack-specific notes (short punchy sign-offs, explicit rollback notes) in section 4.

If genuinely unsure which register fits, default to the lighter one — Rod's docs are notable for restraint, not for reaching for structure they don't need.

## 1. Structural signature (docs only)

Apply these in roughly this order when building a doc:

- **Open with the decision or belief, not the background.** DACIs open with "What decision needs to be made?" Proposals open with the ask, not the history.
- **Name Non-Goals explicitly, as their own section**, and make them do real work (pre-empt a specific likely misreading, not a generic disclaimer). E.g. "Velocity is seen as the arbiter of what plugins people can/should use" as an explicit non-goal.
- **Use hypothesis → prediction framing for anything proposing an experiment or bet**: "We believe X. Prediction: if we do Y, Z will happen." Follow with "What do you have to believe to endorse this plan?" for higher-stakes bets.
- **Bury detail in toggles, not in the main flow.** Meeting notes, edge cases, and "most readers can ignore this" content go under a `{toggle="true"}` block. Say explicitly that it's skippable.
- **Tables for anything comparative** — pricing, ownership, priority definitions. Put a number on things people usually leave vague (e.g. "85% of these projects should be delivered," not "most").
- **One callout box near the top** (💡, ℹ️, or ⭐ icon) giving the reader the one thing they need before the rest makes sense.
- **Table of contents on anything over ~800 words.**
- **Name your own rhetorical device when you use one**, with a link if there's a source: Cunningham's Law, DACI, Hofstadter's Law, Stepping Stones not Milestones, Strangler Fig, "5 So-Whats" (Rod's own remix of 5 Whys).
- **Close on one short sentence that reframes the whole doc** — not a summary paragraph. ("The best time to start was last year, the second best time is now!")

## 2. Voice habits (everywhere — docs and Slack)

- **Hedge visibly rather than assert past your actual knowledge.** "I currently believe, low confidence," "AFAICT," "I don't have a good sense right now," "I suspect." This is a feature, not a weakness — Rod's docs read as more credible because of it, not less.
- **Quantify instead of gesturing.** Not "a lot of the bill" — "58.5% of our AWS bill is now tagged." Not "search is broken sometimes" — "milestone rate is 20–30% per search."
- **Dry humour lives in parentheses, never in the topic sentence.** "(Or maybe not if we're moving the catalogue to a CMS?)" The main clause stays flat and informative; the joke is the aside.
- **Credit people by name, inline, even when driving the doc yourself.** "As Jenn pointed out..." / "@so-and-so, does anyone have context for...?"
- **Frame drafts as drafts, out loud, so nobody over-reads them.** "It's a strawman proposal — please don't read too much into just the words in this doc."
- **Blunt when the content calls for it, but never padded.** Direct critical assessments are delivered plainly, without corporate softening *and* without unnecessary harshness — state the observation, don't decorate it.
- **No swearing in anything shared, drafted, or sent.** It has appeared exactly once across the whole corpus, in the single most private, least-shared personal doc, used for emphasis rather than decoration. Default: never swear in output. If Rod explicitly asks for it in a specific throwaway/personal note, that's his call, not the default.

## 3. Diction

- British spelling throughout: organised, favour, recognise, licence (noun) — including in fast Slack messages, not just polished docs.
- Reach-for words: *cadence, friction, ladder up, shepherd, muscle (as in "build new muscle"), toil, papercuts, blast radius, force multiplier, boring technology, portfolio-based approach.*
- Coin a compact label for a recurring concept rather than using a generic noun: "Friction Shepherd," "Fresh Socks," "junk drawer team," "hyperobject flailing."
- Precise engineering/product jargon is fine and expected — this is written by and for engineers — but decorative jargon with no added precision is not Rod's style.

## 4. Slack-specific notes

- Short. Rarely more than a paragraph unless it's an incident/status update.
- Status and incident updates keep bullets even in Slack — e.g. a root-cause bullet, a fix bullet, a caveat bullet.
- Common sign-offs: "Thanks all!", "LMK if anyone sees issues," "Have a great weekend," "Happy break, friends!"
- Rollback/verification plans get stated explicitly and briefly even in a casual channel post: what changed, expected impact (usually "none"), how to flag a problem.
- Questions to the team are genuinely open, not rhetorical: "Does anyone ever use X?" rather than assuming the answer.

## 5. Quick self-check before sending

- [ ] Does the first sentence say the decision/ask/belief, not the throat-clearing?
- [ ] Is there at least one specific number instead of a vague quantifier?
- [ ] Is uncertainty flagged where it exists, rather than smoothed over?
- [ ] Is anyone else's contribution credited by name if relevant?
- [ ] Does it end on a line that lands, not a recap?
- [ ] No swearing, no unearned jargon, no corporate padding?

If drafting a long doc (>800 words), also check: ToC present, Non-Goals section present if scope could be misread, one framing callout near the top, detail pushed into toggles rather than inline.

# Hunk Review

Hunk is an interactive terminal diff viewer. The TUI is for the user -- do NOT run `hunk diff`, `hunk show`, or other interactive commands directly. Use `hunk session *` CLI commands to inspect and control live sessions through the local daemon.

If no session exists, ask the user to launch Hunk in their terminal first.

## Workflow

```text
1. hunk session list                                    # find live sessions
2. hunk session get --repo .                            # inspect path / repo / source
3. hunk session review --repo . --json                  # inspect file/hunk structure first
4. hunk session review --repo . --include-patch --json  # opt into raw diff text only when needed
5. hunk session context --repo .                        # check current focus when needed
6. hunk session navigate ...                            # move to the right place
7. hunk session reload -- <command>                     # swap contents if needed
8. hunk session comment add ...                         # leave one review note
9. hunk session comment apply ...                       # apply many agent notes in one stdin batch
10. hunk session highlight add ...                      # light up the exact range you are explaining
```

## Session selection

Most session commands accept:

- `--repo <path>` -- match the live session by its current loaded repo root (most common)
- `<session-id>` -- match by exact ID (use when multiple sessions share a repo)
- If only one session exists, it auto-resolves

`reload` also supports:

- `--session-path <path>` -- match the live Hunk window by its current working directory
- `--source <path>` -- load the replacement `diff` / `show` command from a different directory

Use `--source` only for advanced reloads where the live session you want to control is not already associated with the checkout you want to load next. For a normal worktree session, prefer selecting it directly with `--repo /path/to/worktree`.

## Commands

### Inspect

```bash
hunk session list [--json]
hunk session get (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--json]
hunk session context (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--json]
hunk session review (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--include-patch] [--include-notes] [--json]
```

- `get` shows the session `Path`, `Repo`, and `Source`, which helps when choosing between `--repo` and `--session-path`
- `Repo` is what `--repo` matches; `Path` is what `--session-path` matches
- `review --json` returns file and hunk structure by default; add `--include-patch` only when a caller truly needs raw unified diff text
- `review --include-notes` also returns the live review notes alongside the file and hunk structure

### Navigate

```bash
hunk session navigate (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --file <path> (--hunk <n> | --old-line <n> | --new-line <n>) [--json]
hunk session navigate (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --comment <id> [--json]
hunk session navigate (<session-id> | --repo <path>) (--next-comment | --prev-comment) [--json]
```

Absolute navigation requires `--file` and exactly one of `--hunk`, `--new-line`, or `--old-line`:

```bash
hunk session navigate --repo . --file src/App.tsx --hunk 2
hunk session navigate --repo . --file src/App.tsx --new-line 372
hunk session navigate --repo . --file src/App.tsx --old-line 355
```

Exact comment navigation uses the `commentId` returned by `hunk session comment list --json` and does not require `--file`:

```bash
hunk session navigate --repo . --comment comment-1
```

Relative comment navigation jumps between annotated hunks and does not require `--file`:

```bash
hunk session navigate --repo . --next-comment
hunk session navigate --repo . --prev-comment
```

- `--hunk <n>` is 1-based
- `--new-line` / `--old-line` are 1-based line numbers on that diff side
- A line target lands the user's viewport on that exact line (falling back to its hunk when the line is inside a collapsed region); `--hunk` lands on the hunk
- Use either `--next-comment` or `--prev-comment`, not both

### Reload

Swaps the live session's contents. Pass a Hunk review command after `--`:

```bash
hunk session reload (<session-id> | --repo <path> | --session-path <path>) [--source <path>] [--json] -- diff [ref] [-- <pathspec...>]
hunk session reload (<session-id> | --repo <path> | --session-path <path>) [--source <path>] [--json] -- show [ref] [-- <pathspec...>]
```

Examples:

```bash
hunk session reload --repo . -- diff
hunk session reload --repo . -- diff main...feature -- src/ui
hunk session reload --repo . -- show HEAD~1
hunk session reload --repo . -- show HEAD~1 -- README.md
hunk session reload --repo /path/to/worktree -- diff
hunk session reload --session-path /path/to/live-window --source /path/to/other-checkout -- diff
```

- Always include `--` before the nested Hunk command
- `--repo` or `<session-id>` usually selects the session you want
- `--source` is advanced: it does not select the session; it only changes where the replacement review command runs
- If the live session is already showing the target worktree, prefer `hunk session reload --repo /path/to/worktree -- diff`
- `--session-path` targets the live window when you need to keep session selection separate from reload source

### Comments

```bash
hunk session comment add (<session-id> | --repo <path>) (--reply-to <note-id> | --file <path> (--old-line <n> | --new-line <n>)) --summary <text> [--rationale <text>] [--author <name>] [--markup <stml>] [--focus] [--json]
hunk session comment apply (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --stdin [--focus] [--json]
hunk session comment list (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--file <path>] [--type <live|all|ai|agent|user>] [--json]
hunk session comment rm (<session-id> | --repo <path>) <comment-id> [--json]
hunk session comment clear (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--file <path>] [--include-user|--all] --yes [--json]
```

Examples:

```bash
hunk session comment add --repo . --file README.md --new-line 103 --summary "Tighten this wording"
hunk session comment add --repo . --reply-to user:123 --summary "Addressed in the latest revision"
printf '%s\n' '{"comments":[{"filePath":"README.md","newLine":103,"summary":"Tighten this wording"}]}' | hunk session comment apply --repo . --stdin
```

- Agent notes start hidden: the user sees them only after pressing `a` or setting `agent_notes = true`. `--focus` jumps to the new note (or the first note in a batch) and turns agent notes on, so pass it on the first note you leave in a session, or tell the user to press `a`

- Root `comment add` notes require `--file`, `--summary`, and exactly one of `--old-line` or `--new-line`; replies use `--reply-to <note-id>` with `--summary` and inherit the parent's anchor
- `comment apply` items require `summary` plus either `replyTo` by itself or `filePath` with exactly one target such as `hunk`, `hunkNumber`, `oldLine`, or `newLine`
- `comment apply` reads a JSON batch from stdin and validates the full batch before mutating the live session
- `comment list` and `comment clear` accept optional `--file`
- Quote `--summary` and `--rationale` defensively in the shell

### Attention marks

Highlights paint character ranges inside the diff lines the user is looking at — use them to light up the exact expression you are explaining while you narrate.

```bash
hunk session highlight add (<session-id> | --repo <path>) --file <path> (--old-line <n> | --new-line <n>) --start <n> --end <n> [--tone <tone>] [--focus] [--json]
hunk session highlight clear (<session-id> | --repo <path>) [--file <path>] [--json]
```

Examples:

```bash
hunk session highlight add --repo . --file src/App.tsx --new-line 42 --start 6 --end 19
hunk session highlight add --repo . --file src/App.tsx --new-line 42 --start 6 --end 19 --tone warning --focus
hunk session highlight clear --repo .
```

- `highlight add` requires `--file`, exactly one of `--old-line` or `--new-line`, and the `--start` / `--end` offsets
- `--start` is a 0-based inclusive offset into the line's text and `--end` is exclusive, counted in UTF-16 code units — the same `[start, end)` range extensions use
- Tones: `match` (default), `info`, `warning`, `error`, `dim`; `current` renders as reverse video and is best reserved for the one range under discussion
- Pass `--focus` to also land the viewport on the marked line
- Marks survive scrolling, navigation, and reloads that leave the marked file's content unchanged; a reload that changes that file drops its marks, and `highlight clear` removes them explicitly (optionally per `--file`)
- Marks are visual only — pair them with a `comment add` when the explanation should persist as a note

### Experimental rich markup notes (STML)

Only use STML when `hunk session context --json` lists `stml` in `experimentalFeatures`. The user opts into that experience by launching the review with `--experimental`; do not ask a normal session to render markup.

For an opted-in session, `--markup` (or a `markup` field on apply items) renders the note body as STML — a small HTML-like markup for terminal UI (boxes, rows, gauges, badges, lists, code). Keep `--summary` a real sentence: it is the fallback and the `comment list` text.

`hunk diff` includes untracked files by default. If the user wants tracked changes only, reload with `--exclude-untracked`:

```bash
hunk session reload --repo . -- diff --exclude-untracked
```

The user may ask you to walk them through a changeset or review code using Hunk. Start with `hunk session review --json` to understand the file/hunk structure without inflating agent context, then use `--include-patch` only for the files you truly need to read in raw diff form. Use `context` and `navigate` to line up the user's current view before adding comments.

Your role is to narrate: steer the user's view to what matters and leave comments that explain what they're looking at.

1. Load the right content (`reload` if needed)
2. Navigate to the first interesting file / hunk
3. Add a comment explaining what's happening and why
4. If you already have several notes ready, prefer one `comment apply` batch over many separate shell invocations
5. Summarize when done

- Use `highlight add --focus` to steer the user's eyes to the exact expression while you explain it, and `highlight clear` before moving to the next topic

- **"No active Hunk sessions"** -- if Hunk is visibly running, localhost may be blocked by the agent sandbox; retry with network/sandbox escalation. Otherwise ask the user to open Hunk.

- **"Specify exactly one highlight target"** -- pass `highlight add` one of `--old-line` or `--new-line`.
- **"Highlight --end must be greater than --start"** -- offsets are `[start, end)` UTF-16 code units into the line text; end is exclusive.
- **"Specify either --next-comment or --prev-comment, not both."** -- choose one comment-navigation direction.
- **"The session daemon is ..."** -- a `daemon-build-mismatch` (the `--json` error carries `daemon`, `cli`, `attachedSessions`, and `recommendedAction`). # Benchmarks

Reproducible performance and quality measurement for `entire-graph`. The
harness lives in `cmd/graph-bench` (driver) and `internal/bench` (measurement
core); see `bench/README.md` for layout and flags. Its original WP10 plan is
[archived](archive/2026-06-18-entire-graph-v2-implementation-plan.md).

## Provenance of measurement citations in code comments

Comments in `internal/sem/` justify shipped defaults with named measurements: "R30PUB
benchmark payloads", "measured over 79 agent sessions", "eight R30PUB instances"
(`search.go`, `search_callee.go`, `search_editability_test.go`). None of those artifacts
live in this repository, and finding them previously took an org-wide code search.

They live in **`entirehq/graphmark`** (note the org: `entirehq`, not `entireio`), which
carries four suites: Fidelity (`bench.py`, compiler-oracle graph correctness), Tasks
(`bench_tasks.py`, oracle-derived lookups), Agentic-value (`agentic-swebench/`, official
swebench-graded agent runs — `R30PUB_r1` and friends are run labels there, tracked in
`dev/run_validation.py`), and graphify-parity (conversational memory retrieval).
The session-level numbers ("79 agent sessions", token attribution) come from the
agentic-swebench analysis directories.

Free-text `search` ranking is scored by a fifth suite added 2026-09:
`agentic-swebench/tools/recall_suite.py` — gold-file recall@k/MRR over SWE-bench
Multilingual issue text, with committed baselines at this repo's `49a7ef60` and a `--check`
regression gate. Ranking changes here should run it before merging; see
entireio/entire-graph#247 for the measurement history that motivated it, including two
mechanisms that read as plausible and were refuted by it.

## External native-memory comparison

GraphMark's verified `memory-native-v52` release pairs the production prose
search path with Graphify on 300 LOCOMO and 50 LongMemEval-S questions. Entire
Graph scored 0.914 vs. Graphify 0.787 on LOCOMO recall@10, 77.2% vs. 59.3% on
LOCOMO QA accuracy, and 76.0% vs. 68.0% on LongMemEval-S QA accuracy. All
systems used zero build-time LLM credits. Codebase Memory MCP is present in the
release as an off-domain native diagnostic: v0.9.0 indexes the Markdown content
as `Section` nodes but excludes that node type from its public natural-language
BM25 route, so its column is not a third apples-to-apples memory comparison. On
that route it retrieved nothing at all — all 1,050 CMM cells returned a
byte-identical empty context (24 bytes, zero hits), so its QA number is the
shared reader answering from the question alone.

phase. The tune-disjoint holdout is the clean generalization estimate — Entire

            stats[status]["requalified (same file:line:name)"] += 1

**1. The mask is still needed on v0.24.2. Keep it.** It's a single pre-parse pass, not a set of masks like Swift's. It blanks the `cfg_*! { … }` and `cfg_if!` wrappers so the items inside parse as items. That works around how tree-sitter-rust treats macro bodies, not around the grammar's age, so a newer grammar doesn't remove the need. I measured it with a temporary no-mask build, now reverted, on the same clones:

| | With mask | Without mask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Failing files | 3,778 | 3,706 (−72) |
| Symbols | 525,327 | 524,693 (−634) |
| Relations | 1,760,507 | 1,756,908 (−3,599) |

- **What the mask buys:** tokio loses 471 symbols and 3,046 relations without it, and `rust-lang/rust` loses 163 symbols and 553 relations. The other eight repos don't change.
- **What it costs:** it adds 72 failing files (2 in tokio, 70 in `rust-lang/rust`), and none fail only without the mask. Those are `cfg_if!` forms it unwraps imperfectly, such as `target_os = …` conditions, `else if` chains and `unix => {` arms. Even in those files the mask still recovers more symbols than it loses (+9 in tokio's two, +104 in rust's 70).
- **Possible follow-up:** teaching the unwrapper those `cfg_if!` shapes would remove the false failures. I haven't tried it.
- **Not tested:** whether the mask matters equally on the bundled grammar.

**2. Your guess is mostly right.** The net −108 in `rust-lang/rust` is two different things. I compared the symbol IDs of the bundled and v0.24.2 builds, and then matched the "missing" symbols to the "added" ones by file, line and name.

- **Files that parse identically:** zero symbol differences in any file that parses cleanly under both grammars.
- **Files that failed before and parse now:** this is where it's more accurate.
  - 253 of the 262 "missing" symbols here are the same symbol re-qualified. The old grammar's error recovery lost the enclosing `impl`, so methods surfaced as bare `function destroy`. Now they're `method ModuleMap.destroy`.
  - By repo: 170 of 176 in `deno` and 75 of 77 in `rust` are `function` → `method`.
  - The few strays, such as `dladdr` and `setsockopt`, reappear a line later.
  - That's +22 net in `rust-lang/rust`. It means methods carry their type name, which matters for call resolution.
  - `deno`'s +8 comes entirely from this group, including newly visible items like `TlsKeyLookup`.
- **Files that fail under both grammars:** this is the real loss, −130 net in `rust-lang/rust` (205 missing, 75 added), mostly in `library/core/src/cmp.rs` (41), `diagnostic.rs` (19) and `tests/ui/unpretty/exhaustive.rs` (17).
  - **Cause:** I ran four of the worst files in isolation: 256 symbols on the bundled grammar, 174 on v0.24.2.
  - **Syntax:** both grammars choke at the same places on nightly-only syntax: `pub const trait`, `const impl`, struct default field values, `builtin #`, `async gen` and `try bikeshed`.
  - **What differs:** only how much each salvages afterwards. I'd call that an error-recovery lottery, and stable Rust is unlikely to hit it.

So the lost symbols are mostly the old grammar's mis-qualified versions, plus some recovery noise in `rust-lang/rust`'s own nightly-only files. I only did per-symbol analysis on the repos with a delta (`deno`, `rust`). The other eight have identical counts, so a swap there is possible but unlikely.

# Semantic Provider Benchmark

`graph-bench` clones popular real-world repositories per language and measures the
semantic provider over them, emitting a machine-readable performance and quality
report. It originated as the WP10 harness in the
[archived v2 implementation plan](../docs/archive/2026-06-18-entire-graph-v2-implementation-plan.md)
and is meant to be re-run each work phase to track regressions and quality gains.

## Design

- **Clone phase (network) is separate from measurement (no-egress).** Cloning
  uses `git`; the measured analysis runs `BuildProviderSnapshot` with
  `NoNetwork` set, so the path we benchmark is the same local-only path the
  provider guarantees in production.
- **Cloned repos never enter our commits.** They live under `bench/.cache/`,
  which is gitignored.
- **Repeatable.** `bench/repos.json` lists the repositories; `bench/repos.lock.json`
  pins each to an exact commit. Commit the lock file so every phase analyzes the
  same source and the numbers are comparable.

## Tiers

| Tier | Manifest               | Repos               | When                                          |
| ---- | ---------------------- | ------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Fast | `bench/repos.fast.json`| 3/language (72)     | Routine per-phase tracking; runs in minutes.  |
| Full | `bench/repos.json`     | 10/language (240)   | Occasional deep runs; includes mega-repos.    |

The fast tier is a curated subset of the full manifest (no mega-repos like
linux/tensorflow/vscode), so its repos share the same `repos.lock.json` pins and
clone cache — no separate lock needed. The full tier is comprehensive but gated
by a handful of giant repositories and can take 1.5-3 hours.

## Layout

| Path                     | Purpose                                                |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `bench/repos.json`       | Full manifest: 10 popular repos per language.          |
| `bench/repos.fast.json`  | Fast manifest: 3 repos per language (subset of full).  |
| `bench/repos.lock.json`  | Commit pins for reproducibility (covers both tiers).   |
| `bench/.cache/`          | Cloned repositories (gitignored).                      |

# Proposal: vendoring current tree-sitter grammars at ABI 14 (Rust first)

> [!NOTE]
> This draft was prepared by Claude Code, an AI agent, working under Rod
> Begbie's direction. It has not been reviewed by Rod or by the maintainers.
> The measurements come from a throwaway experiment, not from a PR.

## Summary

We should extend `cmd/grammar-refresh` so it can **regenerate** a grammar at
ABI 14 when the upstream release ships a newer ABI, and use that to replace
go-tree-sitter's bundled Rust grammar with tree-sitter-rust v0.24.2.

In the experiment this removed 768 failing files across graph-bench's ten
Rust repositories (4,546 to 3,778), fixed the `&raw const` failure from
issue #345's comment thread, and introduced 2 newly failing files, both
nightly-only syntax in `rust-lang/rust`.

The simpler option, vendoring the newest grammar that is already ABI 14
(v0.23.3), is a net regression on common code and should be rejected.

Three smaller recommendations ride along: keep the existing Rust unwrap mask,
record the generation step in the manifest, and change how the Rust benchmark
is reported (not which release it clones).

## Background

- go-tree-sitter (smacker) has not moved since August 2024, so grammars
  newer than its snapshot have to be vendored. C# (#21) and Swift (#357)
  already are.
- The vendored runtime loads ABI 13 and 14 only. `cmd/grammar-refresh`
  enforces this in `languageABI` and `minABI`/`maxABI`.
- A comment on issue #345 reports the same root cause for Rust: the bundled
  grammar predates raw borrows, so a file containing `&raw const x` or
  `&raw mut x` gets `E_PARSE_ERROR` and Graph cannot list callers of
  anything in it.
- The refresh tool's current refusal message already tells the reader what to
  do: "regenerate it with `tree-sitter generate --abi 14` and vendor the
  result". This proposal makes the tool do that step.

### Why not just take the newest ABI 14 tag

tree-sitter-rust v0.23.3 (1 April 2025) is the newest tag at ABI 14.
v0.24.0 landed the same day and differs from it only by regenerating at
ABI 15. The `&raw` identifier fix ("Raw reference/identifier conflict",
#288, 6 October 2025) shipped in v0.24.1, which is ABI 15.

So the newest usable tag has a bug that the newest release fixed, and the
bug sits next to the very feature we are upgrading for.

## Evidence

All numbers are from `graph-bench -languages Rust` over the ten pinned Rust
clones (53,012 files), full profile, same commits in every run.
"v0.24.2" below means v0.24.2 regenerated at ABI 14.

| Metric | Bundled | v0.23.3 | v0.24.2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Failing files | 4,546 | 4,037 | 3,778 |
| Symbols | 525,427 | 525,373 | 525,327 |
| Relations | 1,760,243 | 1,760,670 | 1,760,507 |

- **v0.23.3** fixed 528 files and broke 19. Seventeen of the 19 are `&raw`
  used as an ordinary variable (`from_str(&raw)`, `match &raw {`), which
  the grammar tries to read as a raw borrow. `tauri` went from `ok` to
  `degraded`.
- **v0.24.2 (ABI 14)** fixed 769 files in the four repositories I diffed per
  file, and broke 2, both in `rust-lang/rust`: `use<Self>` precise
  capturing and a shebang/attribute case. v0.23.3 failed the same two.
  `tauri` returns to `ok`.
- A scratch repository with `&raw const`, `&raw mut` and a variable named
  `raw` fails under the bundled grammar (raw borrow) and v0.23.3 (variable)
  and passes under v0.24.2.
- The existing Rust golden fixtures are unchanged apart from the
  `identity_revision` header, and the Rust unit tests pass.

### What happened to the "missing" symbols

Symbols fall by 100 against the bundled grammar, almost all in
`rust-lang/rust`. I diffed symbol IDs between the bundled and v0.24.2
builds, then matched missing against added symbols by file, line and name.

- In files that parse cleanly under both grammars: **no differences**.
- In files that failed before and parse now: 253 of 262 "missing" symbols
  are the same symbol re-qualified. The old grammar's error recovery lost
  the enclosing `impl`, so methods appeared as bare `function destroy`. They
  are now `method ModuleMap.destroy`.
- In files that fail under both grammars: a net loss of 130 symbols in
  `rust-lang/rust`, from error recovery on nightly-only syntax (`pub const
  trait`, `const impl`, struct default field values, `builtin #`,
  `async gen`, `try bikeshed`). Both grammars choke at the same places and
  differ only in how much they salvage.

I did per-symbol analysis only for `deno` and `rust-lang/rust`, the two
repositories where symbol counts moved. The other eight are identical in
count, so a swap there is possible but unlikely.

### The existing Rust mask is still needed

`maskRustUnsupportedSyntax` blanks `cfg_*! { ... }` and `cfg_if!` wrappers so
the items inside parse as items. This works around how tree-sitter-rust
treats macro bodies, which is not a function of grammar age.

| Metric | With mask | Without mask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Failing files | 3,778 | 3,706 |
| Symbols | 525,327 | 524,693 |
| Relations | 1,760,507 | 1,756,908 |

Without it, tokio loses 471 symbols and 3,046 relations. The mask does add
72 failing files (2 in tokio, 70 in `rust-lang/rust`), all `cfg_if!` shapes
it unwraps imperfectly, but even in those files it recovers more symbols
than it loses.

## Goals and non-goals

Goals:

- Let the refresh tool vendor a grammar whose upstream ABI is above 14.
- Make the generation step recorded, pinned and checkable.
- Land Rust as the first user, with the same evidence standard as Swift.

Non-goals:

- **Upgrading or forking the tree-sitter runtime.** That removes the ABI cap
  but touches the C runtime and every language. #357 already took the
  manifest-plus-tool route; this stays on it.
- **Parsing nightly-only syntax.** `const trait` and friends are upstream
  grammar work.
- **Auditing every other language** for stale grammars. Worth doing, but
  separately.

## Proposed design

### 1. Record generation in the manifest

`internal/sem/grammars/grammars.json` gains optional, additive fields on
each entry:

```json
{
  "language": "rust",
  "reference": "v0.24.2",
  "revision": "77a3747266f4d621d0757825e6b11edcbf991ca5",
  "abi": 14,
  "generated": {
    "tool": "tree-sitter-cli",
    "version": "0.26.7",
    "args": ["generate", "--abi", "14"],
    "source_abi": 15
  }
}
```

`abi` keeps meaning "the ABI of the vendored `parser.c`". Entries without
`generated` behave exactly as today. The tool should also record a SHA-256
per vendored file so an offline check can detect drift (section 3).

The CLI version should default to the one the grammar's own
`package-lock.json` pins. For v0.24.2 that is 0.26.7, which is what I used.

### 2. Tool behaviour

Today the tool fetches the ref, reads `LANGUAGE_VERSION` from
`src/parser.c`, refuses anything outside 13 to 14, and vendors the files
verbatim. The change:

1. Fetch and read the ABI as today. If it is 13 or 14, vendor verbatim.
1. If it is above 14 and the caller passes `-regenerate` (or the manifest
   entry already says `generated`), run the generator in the checkout, then
   re-read the ABI and require it to be 14.
1. Vendor `parser.c`, the scanner, and the three `tree_sitter/` headers from
   the same tag. The regenerated parser compiled against a newer `parser.h`
   (which dropped one typedef) and a newer `array.h` without trouble.
1. Write the `generated` block and file hashes.

Finding the CLI:

- Use `-tree-sitter <path>`, then `$TREE_SITTER`, then `tree-sitter` on
  `PATH`.
- Require `--version` to match the pinned version exactly, and fail with the
  pin command (`npx tree-sitter-cli@0.26.7`, `cargo install`, or `brew`)
  if it does not.
- **Do not install anything automatically.** The tool is already the one
  place that touches the network, and this keeps the supply-chain surface a
  maintainer's explicit choice.

Safety notes for the proposal discussion:

- Generation executes the grammar's `grammar.js` under node. That is
  inherent to `tree-sitter generate`. Mitigations: only ever run it on a
  pinned tag and commit, in the tool's temporary checkout, never in a user
  repository.
- Nothing here changes the provider's no-egress contract. The generated
  files are committed, and building entire-graph still downloads nothing.

### 3. Verification

- **Determinism:** two consecutive runs of `generate --abi 14` on v0.24.2
  gave a byte-identical `parser.c` here (same machine, same CLI version).
  Different machines and CLI versions are untested.
- **Offline check (cheap, per PR):** a `-check` mode that compares vendored
  files against the manifest hashes, as `gen-notices.sh --check` does for
  `NOTICES`.
- **Regenerate check (needs network and node, scheduled or manual):**
  `-verify -lang rust` regenerates and compares against the vendored files.
  If determinism holds across machines this can run in CI; if not, the
  offline check is the guarantee and this one is advisory.
- **Tool tests:** `refresh_test.go` already exercises the tool. Add cases
  using a stub `tree-sitter` script that emits a canned ABI 14 `parser.c`,
  covering: version mismatch, ABI still wrong after generation, and the
  manifest block round-trip.

### 4. Landing Rust

The same shape as the Swift commit:

- `internal/sem/grammars/rust/` with a `binding.go` (as Swift's), and the
  import in `parser.go` switched from `smacker/go-tree-sitter/rust`.
- `IdentityRevision` bump, with the revision comment and test pin. Required
  by the repo's own rule: re-qualifying methods re-keys symbols (253 in the
  two repositories I checked), so cached snapshots must not be reused.
- Regenerated goldens (header-only for the Rust fixtures), `NOTICES`, and a
  CHANGELOG entry.
- Keep `maskRustUnsupportedSyntax`. Optional follow-up: teach the unwrapper
  the `cfg_if!` shapes behind the 72 false failures (`target_os = ...`
  conditions, `else if` chains, `unix => {` arms).

Note that #357 also bumps `IdentityRevision`, so whichever lands second
renumbers. I hit exactly this merging main into #357 (Julia took revision 5).

### 5. Benchmarking

I expected a release tag of the Rust repository to help. It does not, for
two reasons I checked.

- **Reproducibility is already solved.** `repos.lock.json` pins an exact
  commit, and the manifest takes `owner/name@<ref>` for tags if wanted.
  The pin for `rust-lang/rust` is already a fixed commit, not a moving
  nightly.
- **Release tags still contain the unsupported syntax.** `library/core/src/
  cmp.rs` has `pub const trait` at 1.99.1 (the latest release) and does
  not at 1.88.0. The standard library is written against unstable features
  by design.

What actually dominates the number is the test suite. Of the 3,548
remaining parse failures in `rust-lang/rust`:

| Location | Files | Share |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `tests/ui` | 2,578 | 72.7% |
| `src/tools` | 451 | 12.7% |
| `library` | 235 | 6.6% |
| `compiler` | 68 | 1.9% |
| other `tests/*` | 212 | 6.0% |

`tests/ui` is rustc's compile-fail suite, which deliberately contains
invalid and unstable syntax, so 78.6% of the failures are in `tests/`.

Recommendation:

1. Report `rust-lang/rust` twice: all files, and excluding `tests/`.
   Use the second as the headline for grammar work.
1. Optionally move the pin to a named release for readability, but do it in
   its own change so before and after numbers stay comparable.
